summary: The five pillars of Islam are the foundational acts of worship that every Muslim must fulfil: the shahada, salah, zakah, sawm, and hajj. Together they form the practical framework of the Muslim's submission to Allah.
content:
The five pillars of Islam (arkan al-islam) are the acts of worship that constitute the outward framework of the Muslim's submission to Allah. They were established in the hadith: 'Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving zakah, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the House for those who are able' (Bukhari 8, Muslim 16).

The pillars and the six articles of faith together define what it means to be Muslim — the pillars are the outward practice; the articles are the inward belief.

## 1. The Shahada — The Declaration of Faith

'Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah' — I bear witness that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.

The shahada is both the entry into Islam and its ongoing foundation. It is not merely words — it requires knowledge of what it means, certainty in it, acceptance without rejection, compliance, truthfulness, sincerity, and love. Scholars have enumerated seven conditions (shurutt) for the shahada to be valid.

The first part (la ilaha illallah) is the foundational principle of tawhid, negating all false objects of worship and affirming that Allah alone deserves worship. The second part (Muhammadur rasulullah) affirms that the way to worship Allah is exclusively through what the Prophet (peace be upon him) brought.

## 2. Salah — The Ritual Prayer

Five daily prayers are obligatory upon every adult Muslim: Fajr (dawn), Dhuhr (midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), and Isha (night). Each prayer consists of a specific number of rak'ahs (units) and involves standing, bowing, prostrating, and sitting in submission to Allah.

Salah is the most frequently commanded act in the Quran after tawhid. It connects the servant to Allah five times every day and is described as the pillar of the religion: 'The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer' (Tirmidhi 2616 — graded sahih). Abandoning salah entirely is a grave matter; classical scholars differed on whether its abandoner is declared a disbeliever, with the Hanbali school holding the stronger view that deliberate abandonment constitutes kufr.

Salah requires ritual purity (wudu), facing the qiblah (Makkah), and proper intention.

## 3. Zakah — Obligatory Almsgiving

Zakah is a specified percentage of wealth given annually to designated categories of recipients (Quran 9:60): the poor, the destitute, those in debt, those working to collect it, travellers in need, new Muslims, those working to free themselves from slavery (historically), and fi sabilillah (in the way of Allah).

Zakah is due on savings, livestock, agricultural produce, trade goods, and precious metals when they reach the nisab (minimum threshold) and one lunar year has passed. The standard rate for cash and trade goods is 2.5%.

Zakah purifies wealth and the soul. Allah says: 'Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify and cleanse them' (9:103). It is distinct from voluntary sadaqah (charity), which is always encouraged.

## 4. Sawm — Fasting in Ramadan

Every adult Muslim must fast the entire month of Ramadan — abstaining from food, drink, marital relations, and all that breaks the fast from before dawn (Fajr) until sunset (Maghrib). Fasting is an act of submission, gratitude, and spiritual development.

Allah says: 'O you who have believed, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain taqwa' (2:183). The goal is taqwa (God-consciousness and piety), not mere physical deprivation.

Those who are ill, travelling, pregnant, nursing, elderly, or otherwise genuinely unable are exempt and may make up missed fasts (or pay fidya in some cases). See the article on Ramadan for the full treatment of its virtues and acts of worship.

## 5. Hajj — Pilgrimage to Makkah

Hajj is a pilgrimage to the Masjid al-Haram in Makkah and its surrounding sacred sites, obligatory once in a lifetime for every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able. It takes place during the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah.

The rites of Hajj include: wearing the ihram (two seamless white garments, symbolising equality and submission), tawaf (circling the Ka'bah seven times), sa'i (walking between Safa and Marwa), standing on the plain of Arafah (the essential pillar of Hajj), and the symbolic stoning of the devil (rami al-jamarat).

Allah says: 'And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass' (22:27). Hajj is the largest annual gathering of Muslims and a powerful expression of the unity of the ummah.

## The Pillars as an Integrated System

The five pillars are not isolated rituals — they are an integrated system of worship that structures time (five daily prayers, one month of fasting per year, one pilgrimage in a lifetime), wealth (zakah), and identity (shahada). Together, they orient the Muslim's entire life around the worship of Allah.
evidence_quran: Surah al-Baqarah 2:183 — 'O you who have believed, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain taqwa'
Surah at-Tawbah 9:60 — the eight categories entitled to receive zakah
Surah at-Tawbah 9:103 — 'Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify and cleanse them'
Surah al-Hajj 22:27 — 'And proclaim to the people the Hajj'
Surah al-Baqarah 2:43 — 'And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow'
evidence_hadith: Bukhari 8, Muslim 16 — 'Islam is built upon five...' (the foundational hadith of the five pillars)
Tirmidhi 2616 (sahih) — 'The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer'
Bukhari 1521 — 'Whoever performs Hajj and does not engage in marital relations or commit sins will return like the day his mother gave birth to him'
scholar_positions: The five pillars are affirmed by scholarly ijma'. Scholarly differences exist on subsidiary rulings within each pillar (e.g., whether abandoning salah constitutes kufr — Hanbali view: yes if deliberate; Shafi'i/Maliki/Hanafi view: major sin deserving execution but not kufr). The article presents the pillars at the level of consensus; fiqh details are covered in each pillar's dedicated article.
sources: Muslim, Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Iman (Hadith of Jibril and pillars hadith)
Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, Jami' al-'Ulum wal-Hikam
